items.headline: Gold and silver rip higher into Friday's close even as equities rally: gold +1.52% to $4,220.30, silver +3.46% to $61.11, GDX +2.95% to $89.28
items.summary: On verified Friday 9 Oct closes, gold rose 1.52% to $4,220.30/oz and silver jumped 3.46% to $61.11/oz, with the gold-miner ETF GDX up 2.95% to $89.28 -- an unusual combination given equities also rallied broadly the same session, suggesting the move is ETF-flow/structural rather than pure flight-to-safety. Intraday commodity trackers that morning had shown gold/silver a touch lower (around $4,187 and $60.50), so the strength built through the US session. The rally follows the World Gold Council's report of a record $31B in global gold ETF inflows in Q3 2026.
items.actionable: Silver and miners rallying alongside, not against, Friday's risk-on equity session is constructive for the levered silver/miner book -- it reads as a continuation of the structural ETF bid rather than a trade that should be faded when equities are also up.

items.headline: Correction: the rare-earth truce was already extended to Jan 10, 2027, not expiring Nov 10 as previously reported here
items.summary: Correcting this book's prior framing: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced on Sept 23, 2026 that the US-China trade truce -- including the suspension of China's expanded Oct 2025 rare-earth export controls, originally set to lapse Nov 10, 2026 -- has been extended to Jan 10, 2027 following the Trump-Xi summit. The two-month extension is shorter than the 6-12 months many importers had hoped for, and it leaves the underlying April 2025 licensing regime on seven medium/heavy rare earths (samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium, yttrium) fully in force; Chinese rare-earth magnet shipments to the US still fell ~20% month-on-month in August. This supersedes the 'Nov 10 cliff' framing in this book's prior item.
items.actionable: The near-term Nov 10 supply-shock scenario is off the table, which removes a near-dated bullish catalyst for the rare-earth watchlist, but the short two-month rollover (vs. a full-year renewal) and unchanged underlying licensing regime mean the structural non-China-supply thesis for MP/Lynas/Energy Fuels is intact -- reset the calendar alert to Jan 10, 2027 rather than Nov 10.

items.headline: MP Materials to deliver GM's first non-China rare-earth magnets; Lynas inks ~$96m Pentagon offtake
items.summary: MP Materials is about to deliver General Motors' first rare-earth magnets made outside China, from its Texas facility, backed by the Pentagon's $400m preferred-equity stake, a $150m loan, and a 10-year commitment to buy NdPr output at a $110/kg floor. Separately, Lynas Rare Earths agreed to sell roughly $96m of light and heavy rare earths to the US Department of War over four years, referencing the same $110/kg NdPr floor.
items.actionable: Both watchlist names now have government-backed, price-floored revenue streams independent of spot rare-earth pricing and independent of the Jan 10, 2027 truce outcome, which de-risks the long thesis on MP/Lynas either way.

items.headline: Hormuz tanker attacks hit a 'wartime high' even as Trump pursues Iran diplomacy and rules out strikes before midterms
items.summary: USNI News and CNBC reported Oct 9 that tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz have surged to their highest pace of the 2026 Iran war, with 11 tankers hit in the week ended Oct 4 (the most since the conflict began) and five more hit this week, including the UAE-owned 'On Peace,' which injured 12 Indian crew. Separately, Trump said Oct 8 the US was having 'productive discussions' with Iran and would not strike before the Nov 3 midterms, while insisting the US naval blockade of Iranian ports stays in place and claiming record crude volumes are still transiting the strait; Iran's foreign minister is reviewing a US counterproposal to reopen Hormuz within seven days. On the price spine, WTI held near $91.66 and Brent near $104.43 -- still close to the week's spike levels rather than retreating on the diplomacy.
items.actionable: The strike-rate escalating even as Trump talks de-escalation is a reminder that Hormuz risk is not resolving cleanly -- oil staying elevated keeps inflation/Fed-hawkishness pressure alive (headwind for miners via yields) while the attack risk itself remains a latent tail-risk catalyst for a renewed gold/silver safe-haven bid if talks break down.

items.headline: US stocks close out a volatile week with a broad Friday rebound: S&P 500 +0.59% to 7,811.54, Nasdaq +0.64% to 27,366.17, Dow +0.83%, VIX -3.70% to 14.84
items.summary: On verified Friday closes, the S&P 500 gained 0.59% to 7,811.54, the Nasdaq rose 0.64% to 27,366.17, the Dow added 0.83% to 51,654.95, and the Russell 2000 rose 0.46% to 2,806.98, while the VIX fell 3.70% to 14.84, as tech and chip names rebounded and oil eased off its spike on Trump's Iran de-escalation comments. All three major US averages posted weekly gains despite Thursday's selloff, closing not far off record highs heading into earnings season.
items.actionable: The snap-back confirms Thursday's Fear & Greed dip to 38 was a sentiment air-pocket rather than a trend break -- equity risk appetite recovered quickly, but the VIX is still above its recent lows, so treat this as a resumption of the uptrend rather than an all-clear for aggressive re-leveraging.

items.headline: Fed's Waller, Williams and Jefferson signal more hikes ahead but no back-to-back move at the October meeting
items.summary: Speaking in Istanbul Oct 8, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said additional rate hikes will likely be needed to bring inflation to target -- citing 16 of 18 FOMC participants' dot-plot projections for another 2026 hike -- but said hikes 'do not need to come at consecutive meetings.' NY Fed President John Williams said there is 'no need for urgency' and that one further adjustment late this year may be appropriate, while Vice Chair Philip Jefferson confirmed the Fed does not expect to hike again at the upcoming October meeting.
items.actionable: A skipped October hike (now effectively confirmed by three officials) removes a near-term rate-shock risk for the silver/gold-miner and crypto books, but the reaffirmed hawkish year-end bias means the path still points to higher-for-longer -- a near-term relief rally in metals/crypto is plausible, but size for renewed pressure around the December meeting.

items.headline: Xiaomi jumps ~9.7% to HK$25.96 after SkyNomad SUV racks up 70,000 orders in its first month
items.summary: Xiaomi shares surged as much as 9.2-9.7% Friday after the company said its newly launched SkyNomad SUV accumulated more than 70,000 non-refundable orders in its first 30 days on sale, confirming strong demand for its EV push beyond smartphones. The stock was the single biggest contributor to the Hang Seng Index's Friday rebound.
items.actionable: This is a company-specific demand catalyst (EV order volume), not a broad HK tech re-rating, so treat Friday's Xiaomi move as idiosyncratic upside for that name rather than a signal to add broadly across the Hang Seng Tech book.

items.headline: Hang Seng jumps 1.79% to 24,211.35 as financials and internet names rebound together from Thursday's rout
items.summary: The Hang Seng Index closed Friday at 24,211.35, up 425.56 points (+1.79%), rebounding from Thursday's 1.43% fall as investors bought back into names that had sold off over the prior two sessions. Tencent gained ~3.3% to HK$424.80 and Kuaishou rose ~5.5% on internet-sector strength, while HSBC (+~1.8-2.2%) and Standard Chartered (+~1.4%) partially recovered their Thursday declines and SMIC added 1.50% to HK$57.65; easing Hormuz tensions after Trump's no-strikes-before-midterms comments also helped sentiment broadly.
items.actionable: Friday's rebound looks like a genuine bounce off oversold conditions (Thursday's Hang Seng Tech 2-year low) rather than a reversal of the underlying UK-tax/bond-yield pressure on HSBC/StanChart, so treat current levels as a relief bounce and watch whether Tencent/internet strength can hold into next week without a fresh catalyst.

items.headline: SGX banks stabilize Friday (DBS -0.66% to S$73.36, OCBC flat at S$29.00) after JPMorgan flagged Southeast Asian bank earnings risk from surging bond yields
items.summary: On verified closes, DBS eased a further 0.66% to S$73.36 and OCBC was flat at S$29.00 on Friday, a much milder move than Thursday's roughly 4-5% slide, suggesting the global bank selloff is losing momentum locally. The rout had been driven in part by a JPMorgan note (analyst Harsh Wardhan Modi) warning that surging long-bond yields will hurt Q3 earnings for Southeast Asian lenders via mark-to-market trading losses and slower capital-markets activity, with OCBC flagged as more at risk from wealth-fee normalization -- compounding Citi's Oct 7 downgrade of OCBC to Sell.
items.actionable: The much smaller Friday declines versus Thursday's rout suggest the SGX bank selloff is stabilizing even though the underlying NIM/bond-yield concern (JPMorgan, Citi) hasn't been resolved -- watch Q3 earnings prints (expected into November) as the next real test rather than reading Friday's calm as an all-clear.

items.headline: Bitcoin bounces to $82,551.86 (+1.07%) off Thursday's ~$81,845 low, but spot ETF outflows are the largest since June
items.summary: Bitcoin rose 1.07% to $82,551.86 on verified Friday levels, a tentative bounce off Thursday's roughly $81,845 low, even as US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $484.9m in net outflows on Oct 7 -- the largest single-day outflow since June 25 and enough to erase October's prior inflows, led by BlackRock's IBIT (-$207.7m), Fidelity's FBTC (-$105.1m) and ARK's ARKB (-$101.7m). Ether ETFs also shed roughly $506m over the prior five sessions.
items.actionable: The price bounce without accompanying ETF inflows is a weak-footed rally -- institutional flows, not spot price, are the better signal here, so don't treat Friday's bounce alone as confirmation that the multi-day institutional de-risking in BTC/ETH has reversed.
